title: Invisible Maps of Religion
thesis: Religious maps do not merely illustrate belief: by centring sacred cities, orienting bodies toward holy directions and turning pilgrimage into a sequence of stations, they organise lived space before political borders or measured distance become the dominant grammar.
whyThisSite: Terra Chartarum can compare centred world pictures with itinerary maps and city plans, then use the shared timeline, catalogue and room system to show how cosmology, ritual movement and urban memory produce different but interoperable kinds of sacred geography.

claims.claim: Medieval mappaemundi form a varied family of diagrams, lists and world images rather than one uniform projection tradition.
Many mappaemundi place episodes from sacred and classical history in the same field as places, making chronology spatially available.
The Hereford Mappa Mundi places Jerusalem at the centre of a 52-inch geographic circle and includes roughly 420 cities and towns alongside biblical, natural and classical material.
Matthew Paris’s Royal MS 14 C VII prefatory sequence includes an itinerary from London to the Holy Land, organising the route as ordered stations.
The 1475 Rudimentum Novitiorum combines world history with two printed maps, carrying schematic sacred geography into the incunable book.
The essay’s centre, orientation and route vocabularies are analytical descriptions of graphic structure, not claims that every medieval reader interpreted a map identically.
